extracted.intended_audience: researchers, editors, publishing professionals, and readers interested in publication ethics and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: News coverage summarizing the reasons and context for mass journal retractions, focusing on manipulated peer review, paper-mill activity, and publisher investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised/manipulated peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices state articles were "accepted solely on the basis of a compromised peer review process"; manipulated peer review is cited as the reason for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following an investigation by the publisher, all parties concluded acceptance was based on a compromised process and editors therefore retracted the article. Many retraction notices share similar text asserting manipulated peer review as the primary cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerning similarities in format and structure (indicator of coordinated/unnatural submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several retraction notices cited that "a number of articles shared concerning similarities in format and structure," identified by a third party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared similarities in layout, organization, or manuscript structure across multiple submissions can be treated as evidence suggesting coordinated or paper-mill activity and trigger further investigation and potential retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of excessive self-citations
rubrics_metrics.description: At least 21 of the retractions credited a "third party" that found "evidence of excessive self-citations" in the articles' references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual patterns of self-citation (e.g., disproportionate citation of the authors' own work or a narrow set of sources) can be used as supporting evidence of manipulation or unethical citation practices and may be cited in retraction notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper mill activity as a basis for scrutiny and retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and notices referenced papermill activity as contributing to increased submission volumes and problematic publications; prior large-scale retractions have been attributed to paper mills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may attribute sudden increases in submissions and recurring manuscript patterns to paper mills; identification of paper-mill signatures (formulaic manuscripts, repeated templates, fabricated data) can prompt mass retractions and editorial board responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher investigation and third-party alerts as triggers for corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations sometimes started internally but were also prompted by "third party" alerts to the publisher about concerning patterns; publishers conduct investigations and issue retraction notices based on findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers rely on internal review and external whistleblowers/third-party analyses to detect problems. A formal investigation by the publisher that concludes peer-review compromise or other misconduct is used as the basis for retraction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of author responses (non-response or disagreement) in retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly 80 percent of the notices stated the authors did not respond to the notice regarding retraction, with 15 percent of authors disagreeing with the retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices may explicitly record whether authors responded or disagreed; lack of author response does not prevent retraction when the publisher's investigation supports corrective action. Notices often state author disagreement or silence for transparency.
